Seeking Advice on A Two-Day/Overnight Hike

For just a two day hike you should be able to carry all your water and food on you. Try to avoid salty foods or heavy canned goods. Learn to ration your water so you don't piss it out.

It varies by person but you can probably get down into the 50s with just a wind block outer layer and an inner layer that won't be cold if it gets damp.

Avoid light green that attracts bugs.

Tents are warmer the smaller they are.

Good boots, first aid kit, know how to splint an ankle. Hopefully you won't need too but that can get you to a doctor hours faster.

Research What's called the ten Essentials. You need to carry those with you on every single hike you go regardless of distance. Learn to use a map and compass and always have a map of the area or you're hiking in. You sound way too green to be taking on too much right now.

As stated, the two-day thru hike is an eventual goal. It's not THE goal right now. I took quite a few lessons from the first hike we did. Thankfully, I'm documenting those as we speak.

I'm not denying we're green. We are greener than goose shit at this point but lemme tell ya what I took from our first outing.

  1. Footwear. I wore Bates Tactical Boots. That's my every day footwear and it did alright but these things are over a year old. The cushion is beaten down and the soles are a bit worn as well. Both of us needed something more comfy as, after 10 miles on uneven and somewhat uneven and rocky terrain, both of us had our dogs barking at us. Not terribly but enough that it got our attention

  2. Both of us figured (goddamn wrong) that the map at the start of the trail would be easy to follow. Well, that was bullshit too. We should have stopped off and gotten one and taken it with us.

  3. I actually have a decent compass and I didn't think to take that along either.

  4. We didn't get an early enough start. My hiking bud was making lunch for both of us and wanted to do nothing but stop every couple of steps and yak about one thing or another. That delayed us leaving by about two hours. Not good.

  5. We left lunch in the car thinking this was gonna be no more than three hours. That should have been taken with us. We could have stopped off trail at some point, had lunch and kept it moving.

We did do a few things right though.

  1. Walking sticks. Having those kept us from tripping, helped us clear off debris from the trail and kept us upright while providing us with some extra stability. Not only that but they served as great probes for ground that might have been a little too soft or support for those inclines

  2. Water. We did take that. My hiking buddy took a 16 oz bottle of water...that was it. Me? I took a 40 oz Klean Kanteen and stuck it into a Condor H2O pouch which kept it cold through the entire hike.

  3. Hats. Granted, they were just baseball caps but they sufficed and they worked.

  4. Phones. We had signal out there and it was good. Would have used GPS however, not much but trees and barely a clear view of the sky of which to speak but we had a means to call for help if needed. Thankfully, we didn't need it.

You made a lot of mistakes. I taught mountaineering for over 10 years and was also a LRS in the Army. I have seen so many people end up stranded in lost in the woods from what they thought was a short insignificant Day hike. You need to do a lot of self-educating before you even consider doing a two-day trip. There are a ton of online resources but it doesn't matter if you're going on a half mile hike or a 10-mile hike you need to bring with you the 10 Essentials every single time without exception. You need dedicated hiking boots if you're a beginner hiker. You always need to make sure that you inform someone where you're going and when you're expected to be back. If you're planning on going on overnight trips you need to know how to properly store your food at night which is hanging from a tree branch. You need to know things like you do not cook in the same area where you keep your tent, you never keep any food or food wrappers in your pack or in your tent and you never eat in your tent. There's a ton of s*** you need to learn.

It's two days, you don't need water purification and stuff like that. Just bring a couple gallons, you'll be fine.

Beat advice I can give you for hiking that I haven't seen yet: sleeping clothes. Doesn't matter if they're just t-shirt and shorts, you need to bring a pair of clothes to only and explicitly sleep in. Do not wear them for anything other than sleeping, unless it's an emergency and I'll tell you why:

The clothes you wear hiking get covered in sweat. Not a big deal, normally, cause you're going home. The sweat doesn't evaporate from clothes very well, at all, and if you wear them to sleep in then you're basically going to sleep in a very cold area, covered in water. You will fucking freeze like never before, I know from personal experience and it was probably ~65 when I did it.

Oh, also, you've gotta either carry your shit out with you or bring a shovel. So take TP.

Also a magnesium fire starter. And a bit of lint from your dryer in a bag, for kindling. It'll spark up crazy easy.

And one of those space sleeping bags. They're really nice, once you get past the crinkling.

And a map. Compass not really necessary, cause sun rises in the East, but it can be handy to give you an exact heading.

Also, you kinda found out earlier when you got lost but, shit happens. Expect 2 days, plan for 4.

Have fun! Watch out for mountain lions.
